As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking?

Nina Boyarchenko and Leonardo Elias

The size of global corporate bond markets has increased dramatically over the past three decades. As of the end of 2024, nonfinancial corporate bonds issued by U.S. firms accounted for 29 percent of U.S. GDP. In other advanced economies, though bond markets remain smaller than in the U.S., corporate bonds were on average 11 percent of GDP in the same year. This growth is usually read as a shift from bank to market finance. But the ratio of bonds to GDP can rise either because firms take more debt in general, or because firms shift the composition of their debt toward bonds. In this post, we document growth in bonds to GDP for both the U.S. and other advanced economies, and argue that the sources of that growth are different across countries and have changed over time.

Why does the distinction between sources of growth matter? If bond markets grow because firms substitute away from banks, conditions in the bond market govern a larger share of corporate liabilities and bank lending standards a smaller one. That matters because, as we discussed in a prior Liberty Street Economics post, credit conditions in the two markets can be disconnected. If instead bond markets grow because firms borrow more of everything, the balance between the two is unchanged and firms are simply more exposed to both.

How Much Have Corporate Bond Markets Grown?

We start by documenting the overall trends in the size of the corporate bond markets around the world relative to the size of the economy. The chart below plots the time series of nonfinancial debt securities outstanding (that is, corporate bonds issued by nonfinancial firms resident in a country) as a percentage of GDP, for the U.S. and an equal-weighted average of other advanced economies.

Global Corporate Bonds Markets Were Growing Steadily Before the COVID-19 Pandemic

Sources: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Financial Accounts of the United States (Z.1); OECD financial accounts; ICE Data Indices; IMF World Economic Outlook; Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis FRED; authors’ calculations.Notes: This chart plots outstanding debt securities of nonfinancial corporations, at face value, as a percentage of GDP. U.S. data are for the nonfinancial corporate business sector and are reported at face value; for other economies, market values are converted to face value using ICE bond price indices. The other-advanced line is an equal-weighted average across the twenty-three economies with available data: Austria, Belgium, Canada, Croatia, Czechia, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Latvia, Lithuania, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. Countries enter the average as their data begin; the line starts in 1996, when nineteen of the twenty-three are present, and Japan (2005), New Zealand (2007), South Korea (2009), and Spain (2012) enter later.

Starting with the U.S., we see that the corporate bond market grew from 12.2 percent of GDP in 1950 to a peak of 36.2 percent in 2020, nearly a tripling in market size over seventy years. Turning to the other advanced economies, the growth rate of market size has been even faster, with bonds as a percentage of GDP more than doubling over a span of only twenty-four years for the average country, from 5.0 percent in 1996 to 12.2 percent in 2020. While the size of global bond markets is particularly large in 2020 because of COVID-19-pandemic-era issuance, the chart shows that bond markets were growing steadily in the preceding decades. In contrast, relative to GDP, bond market size retreated between 2021 and 2024, mostly driven by outsized GDP growth.

The chart also shows that U.S. corporate bond markets remain large relative to those of other advanced economies. This reflects structural differences between the U.S. financial system, which relies heavily on market-based finance, and the bank-centric financial systems in other advanced economies, notably European countries. In the rest of this post, we decompose the growth in bond market size into the change in bonds outstanding as a percentage of total nonfinancial corporate debt (that is, the composition of corporate debt) and the change in total corporate debt relative to GDP (a measure of how much nonfinancial firms borrow relative to the size of the economy; as a shorthand we will refer to growth in this measure as “credit deepening”).

Before the Pandemic, Credit Deepening Drove Growth in the United States, but Not Elsewhere

The next chart focuses on understanding the pre-pandemic trend in corporate bond market growth at the country level. Starting with the U.S. (left-most bar), we see that most of the growth in the size of the corporate bond market in the U.S. between 1996 and 2019 was due to credit deepening. That is, while the U.S. bond market grew by 9.2 percent of GDP over that twenty-three-year period, total credit to U.S. nonfinancial corporations grew from 41 percent of GDP to 52 percent, accounting for 6.6 percentage points of that growth; the bond share of corporate debt rose more modestly, from 57 percent to 63 percent. Although not reported in the chart below, we can similarly decompose the growth in bonds outstanding relative to GDP over an earlier part of the U.S. sample. Composition played a larger role in that earlier period: between 1980 and 1995, more than 40 percent of the rise in bonds outstanding, from around 15 percent of GDP to 23.5 percent, was due to composition—firms transitioning from bank loans to market-based financing.

Credit Deepening Drove the U.S. Growth; Other Advanced Economies Were a Mix

Sources: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Financial Accounts of the United States (Z.1); OECD financial accounts; ICE Data Indices; IMF World Economic Outlook; Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis FRED; authors’ calculations.Notes: Each bar decomposes a country’s change from 1996 (or earliest observation year if later) to 2019 in corporate bonds outstanding relative to GDP into a composition component (the change in the bond share of corporate debt) and a credit-deepening component (the change in corporate debt relative to GDP), using a midpoint decomposition so that the two sum to the total. Where the two components have opposite signs, one is drawn above zero and the other below; the marker shows the total. Changes are measured from 1996, or from the first year the data become available: Japan 2005, New Zealand 2007, South Korea 2009, and Spain 2012. Debt securities are at face value. U.S. data are for the nonfinancial corporate business sector and are reported at face value; for other economies, market values are converted to face value using ICE bond price indices. Countries are ordered U.S. first, then other advanced economies alphabetically.

Turning to the rest of the advanced economies, we see that the bond market growth in the average advanced economy is a mix between changes in the composition of nonfinancial firm debt and credit deepening. There is, however, substantial heterogeneity across countries. While in the U.S. and Canada increases in bond market size were mostly due to credit deepening, bond market growth in New Zealand, Japan, and Italy was mostly due to a shift in the composition of nonfinancial firm debt from bank to market-based financing. The rest of the countries in our sample are somewhere in between. Notably, the growth of bond markets in France and Germany between 1996 and 2019 was roughly half due to credit deepening and half due to a shift in the composition of debt, while in the UK credit deepening accounted for about three-fifths.

Credit Deepened During the Pandemic

The first chart in this post shows that bonds-to-GDP peaked in 2020–21, across the countries in our sample. With many central banks around the world providing support to corporate borrowing during the COVID-19 pandemic, a natural question to ask is whether corporate borrowing increased overall or whether the unprecedented support provided to the corporate bond market in particular encouraged a shift toward market-based debt. The next chart decomposes the bond market growth between 2019 and 2021 into the debt composition and credit-deepening components. The chart shows that credit deepened in most countries over that period, sixteen of the twenty-four in our sample. Further, for the majority of Eurozone countries, nonfinancial corporate debt shifted toward corporate bonds. For most of the rest of the advanced economies and for the U.S., instead, the share of bonds in corporate debt declined over the pandemic period, so that loans grew even faster than corporate bonds.

The Pandemic Was a Borrowing Event

U.S. data are for the nonfinancial corporate business sector and are reported at face value; for other economies, market values are converted to face value using ICE bond price indices. The Retreat Since 2021 Was Not a Return to Bank Loans

We finally turn to the decline in bond market size relative to GDP since 2021. While total credit to nonfinancial firms continued to grow in nominal terms over the 2021–24 period in every country in our sample, GDP grew even faster. In the U.S., corporate bonds outstanding rose from $8.0 trillion in 2021 to $8.6 trillion in 2024, but GDP grew from $23.7 trillion in 2021 to $29.4 trillion in 2024. The next chart examines whether this slowing of relative growth of bond markets represents also a shift back toward bank loans.

The chart shows that, while bond markets broadly declined relative to GDP, with bonds relative to GDP falling in seventeen of the twenty-four economies in our sample, the source of this decline varied across countries. In the U.S., the UK, and Spain, GDP grew faster than nonfinancial debt, so that the reversal of credit deepening explains more than four-fifths of the post-pandemic decline in bonds outstanding relative to GDP; in the UK and Spain, the bond share of corporate debt actually rose. In other countries, such as Sweden, France, and Austria, a falling bond share accounted for most of the decline. Overall, the bond share of corporate debt fell in only half of the countries in our sample, so the post-pandemic retreat does not represent a broad-based shift back to bank credit.

Bond Markets Shrank Relative to GDP Since 2021

Wrapping Up

Put together, our results show that although bond markets have grown around the world over the past three decades, the speed and sources of that growth have differed across countries. The conclusions we draw in this post depend on how the national accounts are defined: where the boundary of the nonfinancial corporate sector is drawn, whether bonds are valued at market or face value, and which debt instruments are included can each change not just the size but the direction of the trend in the bond share. Firm-level data on individual debt instruments avoid these ambiguities. In a companion Staff Report, we combine national accounts with instrument-level data for firms in more than forty countries to show which firms have moved toward bonds and how they made that transition. The cross-country differences in bond market growth matter for a number of questions: how the composition of credit booms affects the real economy, how much bond market conditions matter for a given economy, and how those conditions affect firms’ ability to finance themselves. We take up these questions in a series of papers: Staff Report, Staff Report, and Staff Report, respectively.

Nina Boyarchenko is a financial research advisor in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s Research and Statistics Group.

Leonardo Elias is a financial research economist in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s Research and Statistics Group.
